title: The Role of Textiles in Space Exploration
description: Read article about Explore how advanced textiles protect astronauts with layered spacesuits, smart sensors, thermal control, radiation shielding, and sustainable materials. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Spacesuits use layered, high-performance textiles to provide pressure, insulation, abrasion resistance, thermal control, and protection from radiation, micrometeoroids, fire, and extreme temperatures.
Future garments could become lighter, more flexible, sensor-enabled, self-repairing, antimicrobial, modular, and more resource-efficient for long deep-space missions.
markdown:
From the spacesuit that protects an astronaut from extreme temperatures to the gloves that allow them to handle equipment, textiles play a critical role in making human spaceflight possible. These are not ordinary fabrics. They are highly engineered materials designed to perform under conditions that clothing on Earth rarely encounters.

In space, a textile may need to resist extreme heat and cold, radiation, abrasion, fire and micrometeoroids while remaining flexible enough for an astronaut to walk, work and move their hands. At the same time, it needs to manage body heat and moisture and provide enough comfort for hours of demanding activity.

A spacesuit is effectively a wearable life-support system. NASA explains that different layers of a spacesuit perform different functions, including maintaining pressure, protecting against space dust and helping regulate the astronaut’s temperature. The complexity is striking: during the Apollo era, the lunar spacesuit and its portable life-support system had an Earth weight of about 180 pounds (82 kg), although that weight was equivalent to roughly 30 pounds on the Moon because of its lower gravity.

As humanity prepares for longer missions to the Moon, Mars and potentially beyond, the role of textiles is becoming even more important. The future of space clothing is moving towards lighter, smarter and more multifunctional materials, and some of these innovations could eventually influence what people wear on Earth.

Why are Textiles so Important in Space?

The human body is naturally adapted to Earth’s atmosphere. Space is a completely different environment. There is no breathable atmosphere outside a spacecraft, temperatures can change dramatically, and astronauts are exposed to radiation and tiny particles travelling at extremely high speeds. Even simple activities such as bending an arm, walking or picking up an object become more complicated when a person is wearing a pressurised spacesuit.

This is where textile engineering becomes essential. A spacesuit is essentially a wearable life-support system. It combines multiple layers of fabrics and specialised materials, each designed to perform a specific function. These layers work together to provide pressure, insulation, protection and mobility.

The result is a garment that does much more than cover the body. It creates a controlled environment around the astronaut, allowing the human body to function in an otherwise hostile environment.

The Spacesuit: A Textile Engineering Marvel

One of the best examples of advanced textiles in space exploration is the spacesuit. A modern extravehicular mobility suit, commonly known as a spacesuit, typically consists of several layers. The Apollo suits demonstrate just how sophisticated this layering can be. Their construction combined materials such as nylon, neoprene-coated nylon, aluminised Mylar, Dacron, Kapton and Teflon-coated fabrics. Different layers were assigned different jobs, from maintaining pressure and providing insulation to protecting against heat, abrasion and micrometeoroids. These layers may include materials designed for pressure retention, thermal insulation, abrasion resistance and protection against the space environment.

The outer layers need to be particularly durable. During a spacewalk, astronauts may come into contact with spacecraft surfaces, tools and other equipment. The material must therefore withstand repeated movement and friction.

At the same time, the suit cannot simply be made extremely thick. Astronauts need sufficient flexibility to perform precise tasks. This creates a major design challenge: how can a textile provide maximum protection without restricting movement? The challenge becomes particularly clear when one looks at the Apollo suit. NASA’s Apollo 11 mission report noted that the suit and backpack weighed about 180 pounds on Earth,1 while internal pressure in the lunar vacuum substantially reduced its flexibility. Modern spacesuit development therefore places considerable emphasis on mobility, joint design and fit. Space agencies and textile researchers have been working on this problem for decades.

Fibres Designed for Extreme Conditions

Ordinary cotton or polyester garments would not be suitable for a spacewalk. Space textiles require materials with specialised properties. Some of the materials used in protective space applications include high-performance fibres such as aramids, including Kevlar and Nomex, as well as other engineered fibres and coatings. NASA has also tested an outer spacesuit material known as Ortho-Fabric, which combines three familiar performance materials: Nomex for flame resistance, Gore-Tex for waterproofing and breathability, and Kevlar for strength. NASA has additionally used Vectran in spacesuit glove palms because of its cut resistance, a useful property when astronauts work around sharp-edged surfaces and equipment.2

Aramid fibres are known for their strength and heat resistance. These properties make them useful in applications where conventional fabrics may fail. Different materials are selected for different parts of the spacesuit. A material that provides excellent thermal protection may not offer the flexibility required for a glove, while a highly flexible textile may not provide sufficient protection against abrasion.

Therefore, spacesuit construction is less about finding one ‘perfect’ fabric and more about creating a carefully engineered textile system.

Protecting Astronauts from Extreme Temperatures

Temperature management is one of the biggest challenges of space exploration. In direct sunlight, surfaces exposed to the Sun can become extremely hot, while shaded areas can become extremely cold. Since there is no atmosphere to distribute heat in the same way as on Earth, astronauts require specialised thermal protection.

Spacesuits therefore use layers that help control heat transfer. Reflective materials can reduce the absorption of solar radiation, while insulating layers help limit heat loss. But thermal protection is only one side of the problem.

An astronaut’s own body generates heat while working. During a spacewalk, physical activity can cause significant heat and sweat production. A suit therefore needs to remove excess body heat as well. This is where liquid cooling garments become important.

Astronauts can wear garments containing networks of small tubes through which cooling water circulates. This system helps draw heat away from the body and transfers it to the spacecraft’s life-support system. In other words, the textile is not simply insulating the astronaut from the environment; it is also helping regulate the astronaut’s internal environment.

The Challenge of Mobility

A spacesuit must be protective, but excessive protection can make movement difficult. Imagine trying to bend your fingers while wearing several layers of stiff material. Now imagine performing delicate repairs while wearing gloves in a vacuum.

This is one of the reasons why spacesuit design involves extensive research into textile flexibility, joint construction and pressure management. Specially designed joints and fabric structures allow astronauts to move their arms, legs and hands more naturally.

Gloves are particularly challenging. Astronauts need protection from extreme temperatures and sharp surfaces while retaining enough dexterity to operate tools and equipment. This is an area where fashion and space engineering share an interesting common ground: fit matters. Just as designers study body movement to create comfortable sportswear, spacesuit designers need to understand how the human body moves under unusual conditions.

Smart Textiles for Astronauts

The future of space textiles is likely to go beyond passive protection. Smart textiles, also known as e-textiles, can integrate sensors and electronic components into fabrics. These technologies could allow clothing to monitor body temperature, heart rate, movement, hydration or other physiological indicators.

For astronauts on long-duration missions, such monitoring could become increasingly valuable. Instead of relying entirely on separate devices, sensors could potentially be integrated directly into garments. The clothing itself could become part of an astronaut’s health-monitoring system. This idea reflects a broader transformation taking place in fashion: garments are increasingly becoming platforms for technology.

Fitness trackers and smartwatches have already introduced consumers to wearable technology. Future space garments could take this concept much further.

Textiles and Radiation Protection

Radiation is another major concern beyond Earth’s protective atmosphere and magnetic field. NASA estimates that a reference mission involving a 180-day journey to Mars, a 500-day stay and another 180-day return could expose astronauts to approximately 1 sievert of radiation3, based on measurements from the Curiosity rover’s Radiation Assessment Detector.

Astronauts in space are exposed to forms of radiation that are significantly different from what people experience at Earth’s surface. The risk becomes even more important for future missions to the Moon and Mars, where astronauts may spend extended periods outside Earth’s protective environment.

Researchers are therefore investigating materials and textile structures that could provide improved radiation protection while remaining wearable. This is a difficult balance. A material designed purely for maximum radiation shielding could be too heavy for practical use. Spacecraft already face strict weight constraints, so every additional kilogram matters.

Future research may therefore focus on lightweight composite materials, advanced fibres and multifunctional textiles that combine several protective properties in a single system.

Protection Against Micrometeoroids

Space may look empty, but it contains tiny particles travelling at enormous speeds. Micrometeoroids and orbital debris can pose a serious risk to spacecraft and astronauts. A spacesuit therefore needs layers capable of resisting penetration and abrasion. This is another area where high-strength fibres become valuable.

The protective layers of a spacesuit are designed to reduce the risk posed by small particles while also protecting against everyday hazards encountered during a spacewalk. The challenge becomes even more complex when designers have to consider weight, flexibility and durability at the same time.

From Space Technology to Earthly Fashion

One of the most fascinating aspects of space textiles is that their influence does not necessarily end in space. Research developed for extreme environments can eventually inspire technologies for use on Earth.

High-performance fibres, thermal regulation, moisture management, protective coatings and smart textiles already have applications in industries such as sportswear, healthcare, defence and outdoor clothing. For example, athletes benefit from fabrics that help manage moisture and body temperature. Workers in hazardous environments need heat- and flame-resistant protective clothing. Medical textiles increasingly incorporate sensors and advanced materials.

This creates an interesting relationship between space technology and fashion. A technology initially developed to solve an astronaut’s problem may eventually inspire a new category of performance clothing for consumers.

What could Future Space Clothing Look like?

As space exploration moves towards longer missions, especially planned lunar and Mars exploration, astronauts may require clothing designed for very different lifestyles. A short spacewalk and a multi-month planetary mission present completely different textile challenge.

This future is already taking shape through NASA’s Artemis programme. Axiom Space’s Axiom Extravehicular Mobility Unit (AxEMU), being developed for Artemis III, is designed with improved mobility, enhanced protection and a wider range of sizing. NASA says the suit is intended to accommodate at least 90 per cent of the US male and female population4, reflecting a growing emphasis on fit and inclusivity in spacesuit design.

Future garments could potentially be:

•   Lighter, reducing the physical burden on astronauts.

•   More Flexible, allowing greater freedom of movement.

•   Temperature-Regulating, responding to changing environmental conditions.

•   Sensor-Enabled, monitoring health and performance.

•   Self-Repairing, reducing the need for frequent replacement.

•   Antimicrobial, helping manage hygiene in closed environments.

•   Modular, allowing damaged components to be replaced instead of replacing the entire garment.

•   Made from Recyclable or Renewable Materials, where practical.

The idea of multifunctional clothing becomes particularly important when resources are limited. On Earth, consumers can own multiple garments for different purposes. On a long space mission, carrying large quantities of clothing is impractical. A future astronaut’s wardrobe may therefore need to do more with less.

Self-Healing and Advanced Materials

One particularly exciting area of research is self-healing materials. Scientists are exploring polymers and other materials capable of repairing small amounts of damage automatically or with minimal intervention. If such technology becomes sufficiently reliable for space applications, it could have major advantages. A small tear in a garment that can repair itself could reduce maintenance requirements and increase the lifespan of protective equipment.

Similarly, researchers are investigating advanced coatings and materials that can respond to changes in temperature or environmental conditions. These developments are still evolving, but they point towards a future where clothing is no longer a passive material. Instead, it could become an active and responsive system.

The Sustainability Question

Space exploration also raises an important question for the future of textiles: how do we make high-performance clothing more sustainable? Spacesuits are complex products containing multiple materials and components. Recycling them is far more complicated than recycling a simple cotton T-shirt. For future missions, however, sustainability could become essential.

When astronauts travel long distances from Earth, transporting replacement clothing and equipment will be expensive and resource-intensive. Longer-lasting garments, repairable components and recyclable materials could therefore become valuable. On future lunar or Martian settlements, researchers may even have to consider producing certain materials locally.

This could lead to a completely new approach to textile manufacturing,
